misconceptions.description: Believing an algorithm or risk score is objective because it is mathematical and therefore free of bias
misconceptions.trigger: teacher trusts a flagging or risk model because it is data-driven rather than human
misconceptions.feedback: A model inherits the bias of its training data and the choices of its designers. Ask what data it learned from and which groups appear underrepresented before trusting its output.

misconceptions.description: Failing to notice that a seemingly neutral input feature encodes race, income, or language status
misconceptions.trigger: teacher accepts a model's features without checking whether ZIP code, attendance, or prior-school data acts as a proxy
misconceptions.feedback: Inspect the inputs for proxies. Features like ZIP code or free-lunch status can stand in for protected characteristics and reproduce inequity even when those characteristics are not named.

misconceptions.description: Judging a model good because its overall accuracy is high while ignoring much worse performance for a subgroup
misconceptions.trigger: teacher cites a single overall accuracy number to defend a tool
misconceptions.feedback: Disaggregate the results. A model that is 90% accurate overall can be 60% accurate for one subgroup. Ask for performance broken out by group before adopting.

misconceptions.description: Letting a model's label override the teacher's direct knowledge of a student's situation
misconceptions.trigger: teacher changes a placement or referral to match a model flag despite contradicting classroom evidence
misconceptions.feedback: The model is one input. Weigh it against your firsthand classroom evidence and intervene to correct the record when the flag conflicts with what you observe.
